name: Village Guilds
description: Hmmmrmm. — Minecraft During his long adventure, Steve stumbled upon a village of villagers. The houses in the village are connected by bidirectional paths. In total, there are $$$n$$$ houses in the village, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. The graph of houses and paths represents a rooted$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ tree$$$^{\text{†}}$$$, rooted at vertex $$$1$$$, where the town hall is located. Consider an arbitrary house $$$v$$$ and its subtree$$$^{\text{‡}}$$$. For each such house $$$v$$$ and each non-negative integer $$$h$$$, consider the set of houses that are in the subtree of $$$v$$$ at a distance exactly $$$h$$$ from $$$v$$$. Such a set will be called a guild . For example, for $$$h=0$$$, the guild will consist only of the vertex $$$v$$$. In the example below, the guilds for the vertex $$$v=4$$$ are shown. The guild for $$$h=0$$$ is marked in red, for $$$h=1$$$ in light blue, and for $$$h=2$$$ in green. Two guilds are considered different if there exists a house that is in one guild and not in the other. Steve wants to know how many different non-empty guilds there are in the tree. Help him with this. $$$^{\text{∗}}$$$A rooted tree is a tree where one vertex is special and called the root. $$$^{\text{†}}$$$A tree is a connected graph without cycles. $$$^{\text{‡}}$$$A subtree of vertex $$$v$$$ is the subgraph of $$$v$$$, all its descendants, and all the edges between them.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of houses in the village. The second line contains $$$n-1$$$ integers $$$p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \le p_i \lt i$$$), where $$$p_i$$$ is the parent of the $$$i$$$-th house in the tree. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output a single integer — the number of different guilds in the village.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2238C — Village Guilds [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
